questions.q: What is the single merit and single fault a story can have, according to Forster?
questions.a: Correct answer: The only merit is making the audience want to know what happens next; the only fault is making them *not* want to know what happens next. A wrong answer (e.g., "good characters" or "beautiful language") reveals the student is confusing the novel's "finer growths" with the story's bare definition as a time-sequence narrative.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Forster says the story is "the lowest and simplest of literary organisms" yet "the highest factor common to all novels."
questions.a: Correct answer: The story is "lowest" because it relies only on primitive curiosity and time-sequence (like a tape-worm), but "highest factor common" because *every* novel must have one—without it, the novel ceases to be intelligible. A wrong answer that calls the story "noble" or "complex" shows the student missed Forster's deliberate demotion of plot to highlight the novel's higher achievements (value, character, truth).

questions.q: Apply Forster's distinction between "life in time" and "life by values" to this real-life moment: "I waited two hours for the bus, but the five-minute conversation with the old man changed how I see my grandfather." Identify which part is "life in time" and which is "life by values."
questions.a: Correct answer: "Waited two hours for the bus" = life in time (chronological, measurable); "five-minute conversation... changed how I see my grandfather" = life by values (measured by intensity/impact, not duration). A wrong answer that labels both as time or both as values shows the student cannot operationalize Forster's dual-allegiance framework.

questions.q: Analyze how Forster uses the Scheherazade analogy to prove that suspense ("what happens next?") is the *only* literary tool that works on "tyrants and savages"—and why this matters for his argument about the story's primacy.
questions.a: Correct answer: Scheherazade survives *only* by withholding the story's next event; her "exquisite descriptions," "tolerant judgements," and "ingenious incidents" are incidental. This proves suspense is the story's irreducible core—the one element that commands attention even from a murderous king. A weak answer merely retells the Scheherazade plot without linking it to Forster's claim that the story is a "naked worm of time" stripped of all finer growths.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Forster believes a good novel should *minimize* the story to maximize the life by values." Defend your judgment with evidence from the text.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The claim is FALSE. Forster insists the novel *must* "cling, however lightly, to the thread of story" and "touch the interminable tape-worm"—denying time inside the novel is a "blunder." The novel *includes* the life by values *using* the story as its backbone, not by discarding it. A wrong "true" judgment reveals the student missed Forster's insistence on the story's *imperative* allegiance, confusing his regret ("I wish that it was not so") with a prescription.

questions.q: Create a 3-sentence "lecture opening" in Forster's conversational style (using "I," "you," "curiously enough") that introduces the primary theme of this essay to a Class 11 audience.
questions.a: Criteria for a good answer: (1) Uses first-person/second-person address; (2) States the theme (story as backbone/tape-worm); (3) Hints at the time vs. value tension. Example: "Curiously enough, if you ask me what a novel does, I'll say—oh dear yes—it tells a story, and I wish it didn't have to, because that story is a tape-worm of time, but without it the novel collapses." A poor answer uses formal academic language ("This essay argues that..."), missing Forster's deliberate colloquialism which *is* part of his method.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The primary theme of Forster's essay "The Story" is the fundamental, inescapable role of the story (plot) as the backbone of the novel—a primitive, time-sequenced narrative driven by suspense ("what happens next?")—and the novel's necessary dual allegiance to both the "life in time" (______ narrative) and the "life by values" (intensity, meaning, and human experience beyond mere chronology).

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're trying to explain to a friend why you couldn't put down a thriller novel even though the writing wasn't "literary"—Forster would say you were responding to the "tape-worm" of story, the primitive human hunger for "what happens next?" that predates ______ itself.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify the primary theme of the essay, trace its development through Forster's analogies (Scheherazade, tape-worm, backbone), and explain how the essay distinguishes between "story" as a low organism and the novel as a complex organism that incorporates value, using textual evidence to support their.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you're trying to explain to a friend why you couldn't put down a thriller novel even though the writing wasn't "literary"—Forster would say you were ______ to the "tape-worm" of story, the primitive human hunger for "what happens next?" that predates literature itself.
